claims.source: Finally, 5′ rapid amplification of cDNA ends (5′RACE) confirmed that the MRP51 transcript produced in the dbp1Δ::kanMX6-ins strains was the same as that seen in wild-type cells, as opposed to the synthetic MRP51 LUTI in the initial cassette-inserted strains (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C).
claims.evidence: Supported by 5' RACE data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C.

claims.claim: Replacing DBP1 with the reversed kanMX6 cassette did not result in a respiratory growth defect.
claims.source: Indeed, we found that replacing DBP1 with the reversed kanMX6 cassette did not result in a respiratory growth defect (Figure 3G; Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: Supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: Use of two new insulated cassettes to replace DBP1 in the forward and reverse orientation confirmed that neither cassette caused a respiratory growth defect, in either orientation.
claims.source: Use of these two new insulated cassettes to replace DBP1 in the forward and reverse orientation confirmed that neither cassette caused a respiratory growth defect, in either orientation (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: Supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: mRNA-seq data revealed stable divergent transcripts stemming from cassette-mediated gene replacements at 5 of 19 loci analyzed.
claims.source: mRNA-seq data revealed stable divergent transcripts stemming from cassette-mediated gene replacements at 5 of these 19 loci (Figure 4A–E).
claims.evidence: Supported by mRNA-seq and ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 4A-E.

claims.claim: For all five cases with stable divergent transcripts, the aberrant transcript was driven from the 5′ end of the resistance cassette.
claims.source: For all five of these examples, the aberrant transcript was driven from the 5′ end of the resistance cassette, like in dbp1Δ::kanMX6 cells (Figure 1E; Figure 4A–E), and consistent with a model whereby bidirectional transcription from the cassette promoter drives aberrant neighboring transcripts.
claims.evidence: Supported by mRNA-seq data shown in Figure 4A-E.

claims.claim: For all four cases where cassette insertions were analyzed in rrp6∆ strain backgrounds with RRP6 controls, a divergent transcript from the site of cassette insertion was observed in rrp6∆ cells that either was absent or less abundant in the RRP6 control.
claims.source: For all of these cases, a divergent transcript from the site of cassette insertion was observed in rrp6∆ cells that either was absent or less abundant in the RRP6 control (Figure 5A–D).
claims.evidence: Supported by published mRNA-seq and tiling array data shown in Figure 5A-D.

claims.claim: For 7/7 (100%) of loci replaced with a variety of cassettes, divergent transcripts were observed from inserted cassettes when nuclear exosome function was absent (achieved by rrp6∆).
claims.source: Thus, for 7/7 (100%) of loci, replaced with a variety of cassettes, divergent transcripts were observed from inserted cassettes when nuclear exosome function was absent (achieved by rrp6∆; Figure 5A–D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C).
claims.evidence: Supported by analysis of published mRNA-seq and tiling array data shown in Figure 5A-D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-C.

claims.claim: Insertion of the S. cerevisiae TEF1 promoter at the DBP1 locus caused an even stronger respiratory growth defect than was observed with the original A. gossypii pTEF.
claims.source: Insertion of the S. cerevisiae TEF1 promoter caused an even stronger respiratory growth defect than was observed with the original A. gossypii pTEF (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: Supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: When the minimal short-pTEF1 was replaced with a longer region of the endogenous promoter region, including the predicted termination site for CUT910, the respiratory growth defect seen with short-pTEF1 insertion was alleviated.
claims.source: Indeed, we found that when the minimal short-pTEF1 was replaced with a longer region of the endogenous promoter region, including the predicted termination site for CUT910 (Xu et al., 2009; Figure 5E; long-pTEF1), the respiratory growth defect seen with short-pTEF1 insertion was alleviated (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: Supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 5E and citation to Xu et al., 2009.

claims.claim: The ~150 bp intergenic region directly following mature SNR13 RNA was sufficient to protect the MRP51 locus from cassette-induced LUTI-based repression.
claims.source: We found that the ~150 bp intergenic region directly following mature SNR13 RNA, which has been shown to induce NNS-based termination in exogenous transcripts, was sufficient to protect the MRP51 locus from cassette-induced LUTI-based repression (Steinmetz et al., 2001; Schaughency et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by growth curve data in Figure 5E showing wild-type growth rates with NNS-kanMX6 cassette insertion, and citations to Steinmetz et al., 2001 and Schaughency et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Wild-type growth rates were observed in non-fermentable carbon sources when the NNS-kanMX6 cassette was inserted at the DBP1 locus.
claims.source: This was demonstrated by the wild-type growth rates observed in non-fermentable carbon sources when the NNS-kanMX6 cassette was inserted at the DBP1 locus (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: Supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: Most, if not all, promoters are bidirectionally active.
claims.source: It is now understood that genomic loci can have complex and linked transcriptional outputs, even in yeast. For example, activity from one transcription start site (TSS) can interfere with the output of nearby TSSs in an adjacent sense or antisense configuration, and that most, if not all, promoters are bidirectionally active (Teodorovic et al., 2007; Neil et al., 2009; Preker et al., 2008; Core et al., 2008; Xu et al., 2009; Seila et al., 2008; Churchman and Weissman, 2011; Jin et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies demonstrating bidirectional promoter activity.

claims.claim: Transcription interference is seen in diverse organisms, including yeast and human cells.
claims.source: Transcription interference is seen in diverse organisms, including yeast and human cells, and can occur between TSSs driving coding or non-coding RNAs and controlling both transcript isoform identity and transcript levels (Chia et al., 2017; Hirschman et al., 1988; Martens et al., 2004; van Werven et al., 2012; Hongay et al., 2006; Hausler and Somerville, 1979; Adhya and Gottesman, 1982; Proudfoot, 1986; Boussadia et al., 1997; Emerman and Temin, 1984; Corbin and Maniatis, 1989; Struhl, 1985).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies demonstrating transcription interference in various organisms.

claims.claim: For genes regulated by LUTI-based strategy, 5′ extended LUTIs are transcribed in place of canonical mRNAs to temporally downregulate protein synthesis.
claims.source: For genes regulated by this strategy, 5′ extended LUTIs are transcribed in place of canonical mRNAs to temporally downregulate protein synthesis (Chia et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2017; Cheng et al., 2018; Van Dalfsen et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to studies describing LUTI-based regulation.

claims.claim: Use of an upstream alternate TSS represses transcription from the canonical TSS in cis via transcriptional interference in LUTI-based regulation.
claims.source: Here, use of an upstream alternate TSS represses transcription from the canonical TSS in cis via transcriptional interference (Chia et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Chia et al., 2017 describing LUTI mechanism.

claims.claim: Translation of the main ORF-encoded protein products from LUTIs are repressed by translation of competitive AUG-initiated upstream ORFs (uORFs).
claims.source: In concert, translation of the main ORF-encoded protein products from LUTIs are repressed by translation of competitive AUG-initiated upstream ORFs (uORFs) (Chen et al., 2017; Wethmar, 2014; Barbosa et al., 2013; Hinnebusch et al., 2016; Law et al., 2005; Brar et al., 2012; Cheng et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies describing uORF-mediated translational repression.

claims.claim: Natural LUTI-based regulation has been shown to modulate gene expression for many genes during meiosis and the unfolded protein response in yeast.
claims.source: Natural LUTI-based regulation has been shown to modulate gene expression for many genes during meiosis and the unfolded protein response in yeast (Chen et al., 2017; Cheng et al., 2018; Van Dalfsen et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to studies demonstrating LUTI-based regulation in specific biological contexts.

claims.claim: Features of LUTI-based regulation are highly conserved across eukaryotes, and evidence suggests the presence of this regulation in more complex species, such as humans and algae.
claims.source: Furthermore, features of LUTI-based regulation are highly conserved across eukaryotes, and evidence suggests the presence of this regulation in more complex species, such as humans and algae (Hollerer et al., 2019; Sehgal et al., 2008; Moseley et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to studies showing LUTI-like regulation in diverse eukaryotes.

claims.claim: Analyses of mutant phenotypes detected in global studies of the yeast deletion collection revealed effects that appeared to result from neighboring gene mis-regulation, termed 'the neighboring gene effect' (NGE).
claims.source: However, analyses of mutant phenotypes detected in global studies of the collection of strains in which each non-essential yeast ORF is replaced with a kanMX cassette revealed effects that appeared to result from neighboring gene mis-regulation, termed 'the neighboring gene effect' (NGE) (Ben-Shitrit et al., 2012; Atias et al., 2016; Egorov et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to studies identifying the neighboring gene effect.

claims.claim: The neighboring gene effect is caused by overlap of the deleted ORF with a regulatory region for the neighboring gene in a subset of cases.
claims.source: This is caused by overlap of the deleted ORF with a regulatory region for the neighboring gene in a subset of cases, as just one of several problems that resulted from the large-scale nature of the effort required to create the deletion collection (Ben-Shitrit et al., 2012; Hughes et al., 2000; Teng et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to studies analyzing the deletion collection.

claims.claim: Most cases of the NGE remain unexplained.
claims.source: However, most cases of the NGE remain unexplained, and this lack of mechanistic understanding makes it unclear how prevalent this effect is in traditional small-scale laboratory studies, and how to prevent it.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field prior to this study.

claims.claim: Budding yeast was the first eukaryotic organism in which targeted genome engineering became highly facile, thanks to the development of a one-step PCR-based editing strategy.
claims.source: Budding yeast was the first eukaryotic organism in which this became highly facile, thanks to the development of a one-step PCR-based editing strategy, frequently used with a shared toolkit of selection cassettes (Longtine et al., 1998; Wach et al., 1997; Wach et al., 1994; Baudin et al., 1993; Lorenz et al., 1995).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to foundational studies developing PCR-based editing strategies.

claims.claim: The yeast deletion collection was created using selection-mediated genome editing strategies.
claims.source: These tools became common, routinely used by thousands of labs as well as to enable large global endeavors, such as creation of the yeast deletion collection (Giaever et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Giaever et al., 2002 describing the yeast deletion collection.

claims.claim: Selection-mediated editing strategies have remained commonplace despite the development of CRISPR/Cas9-based editing methods.
claims.source: Because of the high fidelity, ease of use, and rapid nature of this selection-mediated strategy, it has remained commonplace despite the development of methods allowing non-selection-marked mutations that include CRISPR/Cas9-based editing (Jinek et al., 2012; Güldener et al., 1996; Gray et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to alternative editing methods and the continued use of selection-mediated strategies.

claims.claim: MRP51 encodes a mitochondrial small subunit ribosome protein (mt-SSU).
claims.source: We next sought to determine whether the mutant phenotypes we observed in dbp1Δ::kanMX6 cells were due to loss of DBP1 function or resistance cassette-dependent mis-regulation of MRP51, a gene encoding a mitochondrial small subunit ribosome protein (mt-SSU) (Green-Willms et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Green-Willms et al., 1998 describing MRP51 function.

claims.claim: Measurement of radioactive amino acid incorporation rates revealed a 24% decrease in bulk translation in dbp1Δ::kanMX6 cells.
claims.source: Consistent with this finding, measurement of radioactive amino acid incorporation rates revealed a 24% decrease in bulk translation in dbp1Δ::kanMX6 cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: Supported by radioactive amino acid incorporation assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: When individual cytoplasmic SSU proteins are lost, free cytoplasmic 60S LSUs accumulate, presumably a result of their inability to find an SSU to complex with and form fully assembled 80S species.
claims.source: A previous study from our laboratory observed that when individual cytoplasmic SSU proteins are lost, free cytoplasmic 60S LSUs accumulate, presumably a result of their inability to find an SSU to complex with and form fully assembled 80S species (Cheng et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Cheng et al., 2019 describing ribosome assembly defects.

claims.claim: Mitochondrial dysfunction and translation rates have both previously been shown to impact the TOR pathway and thus influence global translation.
claims.source: Mitochondrial dysfunction and translation rates have both previously been shown to impact the TOR pathway and thus influence global translation (Gao et al., 2016; Jazwinski, 2013; Raught et al., 2001; Topf et al., 2019), consistent with our findings.
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to studies linking mitochondrial function and TOR pathway to translation.

claims.claim: The bidirectional nature of commonly used expression cassette promoters, including pTEF in yeast, and the CMV, eEF1α, and SV40 promoters in mammalian systems, has long been known.
claims.source: The bidirectional nature of commonly used expression cassette promoters, including pTEF in yeast, and the CMV, eEF1α, and SV40 promoters in mammalian systems, has long been known (Curtin et al., 2008; Gidoni et al., 1985).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to studies demonstrating bidirectional promoter activity.

claims.claim: One study that analyzed mutants generated with kanMX modules estimated that replacement at as many as 20% of loci may cause neighboring gene mis-regulation.
claims.source: One study that analyzed mutants generated with kanMX modules estimated that replacement at as many as 20% of loci may cause neighboring gene mis-regulation, and ~10% of deletion collection strains have been estimated to demonstrate non-specific phenotypes in genetic interaction data that could be attributed to neighboring gene mis-regulation (Ben-Shitrit et al., 2012; Atias et al., 2016; Egorov et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to studies estimating the prevalence of neighboring gene effects.

claims.claim: A recent study focused on protein quantification of each yeast deletion collection strain found that one of the most significant factors determining whether a specific protein's abundance would change following deletion of a gene encoding another protein was whether the genes encoding the protein pair were genomic neighbors.
claims.source: A recent study focused on protein quantification of each yeast deletion collection strain found that one of the most significant factors determining whether a specific protein's abundance would change following deletion of a gene encoding another protein was whether the genes encoding the protein pair were genomic neighbors (Messner et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Messner et al., 2022 analyzing protein abundance in deletion collection.

claims.claim: All previously reported examples of the NGE focused only on integrations of kanMX modules.
claims.source: It is important to note that all previously reported examples of the NGE, including those noted here, focused only on integrations of kanMX modules (Ben-Shitrit et al., 2012; Atias et al., 2016; Egorov et al., 2021; Makeeva et al., 2019; Messner et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to studies analyzing NGE with kanMX modules.

claims.claim: Stable cassette-driven divergent transcripts were detected in ~30% of cassette-inserted loci.
claims.source: While we find that stable cassette-driven divergent transcripts were detected in ~30% of cassette-inserted loci, all cassette-inserted loci have detectable divergent transcripts in cells lacking nuclear exosome-mediated RNA decay.
claims.evidence: Supported by analysis of mRNA-seq data from multiple cassette-inserted strains showing stable divergent transcripts at 6/20 loci (~30%).

claims.claim: All cassette-inserted loci have detectable divergent transcripts in cells lacking nuclear exosome-mediated RNA decay.
claims.source: While we find that stable cassette-driven divergent transcripts were detected in ~30% of cassette-inserted loci, all cassette-inserted loci have detectable divergent transcripts in cells lacking nuclear exosome-mediated RNA decay.
claims.evidence: Supported by analysis showing divergent transcripts at 7/7 (100%) of cassette-inserted loci in rrp6Δ backgrounds.

claims.claim: Divergent transcription results ubiquitously from expression cassette insertion.
claims.source: Thus, our data suggest that divergent transcription results ubiquitously from expression cassette insertion, but features—including transcription termination sequences adjacent to cassette insertion—can naturally mitigate off-target neighboring gene mis-regulation.
claims.evidence: Inferred from data showing divergent transcripts at all cassette-inserted loci in rrp6Δ backgrounds.

claims.claim: The nuclear exosome activity is likely to be a major contributor to masking aberrant transcripts from cassette insertion.
claims.source: Although NMD might be expected to target a subset of aberrant transcripts that reach the cytosol, nuclear exosome activity seemed likely to be a more major contributor (Hug et al., 2016; Gudipati et al., 2012; Wyers et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that divergent transcripts are detected at all cassette-inserted loci in rrp6Δ backgrounds but only ~30% in wild-type, and supported by citations to studies on nuclear exosome function.

claims.claim: The 'NNS' pathway—named for complex subunits Nrd1, Nab3, and Sen1—leads to termination of most divergent transcripts and their rapid degradation by the Rrp6/exosome.
claims.source: It subsequently became clear that an alternative transcription termination mechanism, the 'NNS' pathway—named for complex subunits Nrd1, Nab3, and Sen1—leads to termination of most divergent transcripts and their rapid degradation by the Rrp6/exosome (Gudipati et al., 2012; Porrua and Libri, 2015; Wyers et al., 2005; Schulz et al., 2013; Steinmetz et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to studies describing the NNS pathway and its role in divergent transcript termination.

claims.claim: S. cerevisiae pTEF1 drives a divergent transcript (cryptic unstable transcript 910; 'CUT910') that is unstable due to Rrp6/exosome activity at its endogenous locus.
claims.source: Even at its endogenous locus, S. cerevisiae pTEF1 drives a divergent transcript (cryptic unstable transcript 910; 'CUT910') that is unstable due to Rrp6/exosome activity (Figure 5E; Xu et al., 2009), which degrades NNS-terminated divergent transcripts (Fox et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Xu et al., 2009 and data shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: The early termination and degradation of CUT910 presumably protects the neighboring locus MRL1 from transcription interference.
claims.source: The early termination and degradation of CUT910 presumably protects the neighboring locus MRL1 from transcription interference (Xu et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that CUT910 is terminated early and supported by citation to Xu et al., 2009.

claims.claim: Neighboring gene disruption by divergent transcripts resulting from bidirectional pTEF1 (or pTEF) activity at expression cassette insertion sites is partially a result of the use of a 'minimal' promoter region.
claims.source: We thus hypothesized that neighboring gene disruption by divergent transcripts resulting from bidirectional pTEF1 (or pTEF) activity at expression cassette insertion sites is partially a result of the use of a 'minimal' promoter region.
claims.evidence: Inferred from experiments showing that longer pTEF1 regions with termination signals prevent off-target effects.

claims.claim: The minimal promoter region is devoid of its larger natural context and evolved failsafe mechanisms, including NNS-based termination signals, which prevent bidirectional transcripts from interfering with neighboring loci.
claims.source: While this region is competent to drive transcription of a transgene, it is devoid of its larger natural context and evolved failsafe mechanisms, including NNS-based termination signals, which prevent bidirectional transcripts from interfering with neighboring loci (Schulz et al., 2013; Porrua and Libri, 2015).
claims.evidence: Inferred from experimental results and supported by citations to studies on NNS termination.

claims.claim: The off-target effect from cassette insertion is a result of porting a minimal pTEF1 out of its native context, which leads to unmasking, in some insertion sites, of strong divergent transcript production.
claims.source: We concluded that the off-target effect from cassette insertion is a result of porting a minimal pTEF1 out of its native context, which leads to unmasking, in some insertion sites, of strong divergent transcript production.
claims.evidence: Inferred from experiments showing that longer pTEF1 regions with natural termination signals prevent off-target effects.

claims.claim: Naturally occurring NNS termination sites may be an important contributing factor in determining which loci are sensitive to the cassette-driven NGE.
claims.source: These data suggested that naturally occurring NNS termination sites may be an important contributing factor in determining which loci are sensitive to the cassette-driven NGE.
claims.evidence: Inferred from observations that divergent transcripts are short at many loci and experiments showing NNS termination can prevent off-target effects.

claims.claim: Predictions of naturally occurring NNS termination signals based on sequence alone is difficult.
claims.source: Though short binding preference motifs have been determined for the NNS complex, predictions of naturally occurring NNS termination signals based on sequence alone is difficult (Porrua and Libri, 2015; Carroll et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to studies on NNS complex binding motifs.

claims.claim: LUTI-based neighboring gene disruption requires the adjacent gene to be in a 'head-to-head' orientation, the presence of repressive uORFs upstream of the coding sequence, and a continuous divergent transcript containing the entire ORF of the repressed gene.
claims.source: LUTI-based neighboring gene disruption requires the adjacent gene to be in a 'head-to-head' orientation, the presence of repressive uORFs upstream of the coding sequence, and a continuous divergent transcript containing the entire ORF of the repressed gene (Chia et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2017; Cheng et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to studies describing LUTI-based regulation requirements.

claims.claim: Cassette-driven transcription interference can occur regardless of the presence of repressive uORFs upstream of the neighboring coding sequence, does not require the divergent transcript to be continuous over the neighboring ORF, and can act on genes in either orientation to the inserted cassette.
claims.source: Cassette-driven transcription interference, however, can occur regardless of the presence of repressive uORFs upstream of the neighboring coding sequence, does not require the divergent transcript to be continuous over the neighboring ORF, and can act on genes in either orientation to the inserted cassette (Chia et al., 2017; Hirschman et al., 1988; Martens et al., 2004; van Werven et al., 2012; Hongay et al., 2006; Hausler and Somerville, 1979; Adhya and Gottesman, 1982; Proudfoot, 1986; Boussadia et al., 1997; Emerman and Temin, 1984; Corbin and Maniatis, 1989).
claims.evidence: Inferred from comparison of LUTI-based and transcription interference mechanisms, supported by citations.

claims.claim: In haploid cells, induction into meiosis is blocked by the expression of two separate non-coding RNAs that repress an antisense mRNA (RME2/IME4) or a downstream sense RNA (IRT1/IME1) via transcription interference.
claims.source: For example, in haploid cells, induction into meiosis is blocked by the expression of two separate non-coding RNAs that repress an antisense mRNA (RME2/IME4) or a downstream sense RNA (IRT1/IME1) via transcription interference (Hongay et al., 2006; van Werven et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to studies describing transcription interference in meiosis regulation.

claims.claim: Transcription interference between loci can be effective over large distances, like the ~1800 nt span over which transcription of the repressive IRT1 long non-coding RNA represses IME1.
claims.source: Transcription interference between loci can be effective over large distances, like the ~1800 nt span over which transcription of the repressive IRT1 long non-coding RNA represses IME1 (van Werven et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to van Werven et al., 2012 describing long-range transcription interference.

claims.claim: The type of cassette-mediated off-target effect in this study is difficult to detect or predict by sequence alone.
claims.source: The type of cassette-mediated off-target effect in this study is difficult to detect or predict by sequence alone.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the complexity of factors determining off-target effects and the need for experimental validation.

claims.claim: Even the lack of an observable stable divergent transcript is not sufficient to conclude wild-type regulation from a cassette-adjacent gene because disruption can occur regardless of the transcript's stability.
claims.source: Additionally, our data suggest that at as many as 70% of cassette-inserted loci, divergent transcripts are produced but degraded by the nuclear exosome, meaning that even the lack of an observable stable divergent transcript is not sufficient to conclude wild-type regulation from a cassette-adjacent gene because disruption can occur regardless of the transcript's stability.
claims.evidence: Inferred from data showing divergent transcripts at all loci in rrp6Δ backgrounds but only ~30% in wild-type.

claims.claim: Condition-specific manifestation of the cassette-driven divergent transcription at the DBP1/MRP51 locus was observed.
claims.source: Consistently, we observed condition-specific manifestation of the cassette-driven divergent transcription at the DBP1/MRP51 locus.
claims.evidence: Inferred from observations that MRP51 mis-regulation was detected in meiotic cells and that adjacent genes in other cassette-inserted loci were lowly expressed under surveyed conditions.

claims.claim: For 3/5 additional potential NGE cases with detectable aberrant transcripts in exosome proficient cells, adjacent genes were lowly expressed, even in wild-type cells under the conditions surveyed.
claims.source: For 3/5 additional potential NGE cases with detectable aberrant transcripts in exosome proficient cells (Figure 4), adjacent genes were lowly expressed, even in wild-type cells under the conditions surveyed.
claims.evidence: Supported by ribosome profiling and mRNA-seq data shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: It is currently not possible to predict when and where cassette insertion would result in mis-regulation severe enough to mislead studies.
claims.source: Considering the number of factors affecting whether cassette adjacent genes are mis-regulated, we argue that it is currently not possible to predict when and where cassette insertion would result in mis-regulation severe enough to mislead studies.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the complexity of factors determining off-target effects demonstrated in the study.

claims.claim: Complementation-based rescue experiments allowed identification of the unexpected regulation in the case of DBP1 disruption.
claims.source: Despite this complexity, complementation-based rescue experiments—namely single-copy insertion of the deleted gene with its entire endogenous regulatory region at another locus—allowed us to identify the unexpected regulation in the case of DBP1 disruption, and should be more commonly used to confirm phenotypes.
claims.evidence: Supported by rescue experiments showing that Mrp51, but not Dbp1, rescued phenotypes.

claims.claim: Seamless deletions such as those created with the CRISPR/Cas9 approach avoid cassette insertions, but can still result in changes to the local environment of adjacent genes, potentially resulting in off-target effects.
claims.source: Seamless deletions such as those created with the CRISPR/Cas9 approach avoid cassette insertions, but can still result in changes to the local environment of adjacent genes, potentially resulting in off-target effects (Jinek et al., 2012; Güldener et al., 1996; Gray et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to CRISPR/Cas9 methods and observation of novel ORF translation in markerless dbp1Δ.

claims.claim: For the case of a markerless CRISPR/Cas9-based deletion of the DBP1 ORF, translation of a previously untranslated ORF within the mutant transcript containing only the DBP1 5′ and 3′ UTR was observed.
claims.source: For the case of a markerless CRISPR/Cas9-based deletion of the DBP1 ORF, we observed translation of a previously untranslated ORF within the mutant transcript containing only the DBP1 5′ and 3′ UTR (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: Supported by ribosome profiling and mRNA-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Translation of novel ORFs in markerless deletions could cause misleading neomorphic mutant phenotypes, not linked to loss of function of the deleted ORF.
claims.source: One could imagine that in cases like these, translation of novel ORFs could also cause misleading neomorphic mutant phenotypes, not linked to loss of function of the deleted ORF.
claims.evidence: Inferred from observation of novel ORF translation in markerless dbp1Δ.

claims.claim: Even well controlled genomic changes can have unintended consequences on the translation of neighboring coding sequences.
claims.source: These data highlight the point that even well controlled genomic changes can have unintended consequences on the translation of neighboring coding sequences, and emphasize the value of careful analysis of gene expression from loci neighboring those that are manipulated.
claims.evidence: Inferred from observations of off-target effects with both cassette-mediated and markerless deletions.

claims.claim: Two-step strategies to isolate mutants free of selection cassettes have been described but are often used in the context of allowing subsequent re-use of auxotrophic markers and cassettes.
claims.source: We note that two-step strategies to isolate mutants free of selection cassettes have been described but are often used the context of allowing subsequent re-use of auxotrophic markers and cassettes (Güldener et al., 1996; Gray et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to studies describing two-step strategies.

claims.claim: The Cre/loxP system can be used to excise resistance cassettes following mutation isolation.
claims.source: One example of this uses the Cre/loxP system to excise resistance cassettes following mutation isolation (Güldener et al., 1996).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Güldener et al., 1996 describing the Cre/loxP system.

claims.claim: The Cre/loxP strategy can prevent neighboring gene disruption by cassettes, but it is slower and more labor intensive than a single step process.
claims.source: While this strategy can prevent neighboring gene disruption by cassettes, it is slower and more labor intensive than a single step process, and thus may not be commonly utilized to its full potential.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the nature of two-step strategies and observation that loxP-flanked cassettes were not excised in some published studies.

claims.claim: In two datasets analyzed for cassette-driven divergent transcripts in strain backgrounds deficient for exosome-mediated RNA decay, cassette integrated mutants contained flanking loxP sites that were not utilized to excise the cassette.
claims.source: For example, in two datasets we analyzed for cassette-driven divergent transcripts in strain backgrounds deficient for exosome-mediated RNA decay, cassette integrated mutants contained flanking loxP sites that were not utilized to excise the cassette (Schmidt et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by analysis of published data from Schmidt et al., 2012.

claims.claim: Use of a single-step 'insulated' cassette for genome editing maintains the efficiency of the originally designed system, while preventing the potentially catastrophic off-target effects that disruption of neighboring gene expression can cause.
claims.source: Use of a single-step 'insulated' cassette for genome editing maintains the efficiency of the originally designed system, while preventing the potentially catastrophic off-target effects that disruption of neighboring gene expression can cause.
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data showing that insulated cassettes prevent off-target effects while maintaining ease of use.

claims.claim: All the key factors behind the cassette-induced off-target effects described in this study are conserved in higher eukaryotes.
claims.source: While our study was limited to yeast, all the key factors behind the cassette-induced off-target effects described here are conserved in higher eukaryotes.
claims.evidence: Inferred from knowledge of conserved features like bidirectional promoters and transcription interference in eukaryotes.

claims.claim: Genome-editing-driven transcriptional interference, including LUTI-based repression, is likely to occur in other organisms.
claims.source: Because of this, we hypothesize that genome-editing-driven transcriptional interference, including LUTI-based repression, is likely to occur in other organisms.

claims.claim: Promoters in yeast, mammals, and other eukaryotes are inherently bidirectional.

results.result: Replacement of DBP1 with a kanMX6 cassette causes reduced MRP51 expression through production of a 5' extended transcript containing translated uORFs, resulting in decreased Mrp51 protein levels despite increased mRNA abundance.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C7, C8, and C9 collectively demonstrate that kanMX6 insertion at DBP1 leads to MRP51 mis-regulation through a LUTI mechanism. The data show 8.4-fold reduced translation despite 1.8-fold increased mRNA (C7), presence of 3 translated uORFs in the extended transcript (C8), and reduced Mrp51 protein levels by western blot (C9), providing converging evidence for the mechanism.

results.result: The MRP51 mis-regulation phenotype is reproducible across different cassettes and strain backgrounds, as demonstrated by similar effects with hphMX4 insertion in S288C background.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C12 show that hphMX4 cassette insertion causes similar MRP51 mis-regulation (4.4-fold reduced translation, extended transcript with uORFs) in an independent study using a different strain background and cassette type, confirming the generality of the phenomenon beyond the initial observation.

results.result: All observed phenotypes in dbp1Δ::kanMX6 cells result from MRP51 mis-regulation rather than loss of Dbp1 function, as demonstrated by rescue experiments showing that exogenous Mrp51, but not Dbp1, restores wild-type phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C18-C22 provide strong complementation evidence that phenotypes are due to MRP51 mis-regulation. Exogenous Mrp51 rescues all respiratory growth defects (C19), sporulation defects (C20), and polysome profiles (C21), while exogenous Dbp1 at wild-type levels (C22) fails to rescue (C18), definitively establishing causality.

results.result: dbp1Δ::kanMX6 cells exhibit reduced global translation rates and accumulation of mitochondrial large ribosomal subunits, consistent with mitochondrial dysfunction due to reduced Mrp51 (a mitochondrial small subunit protein).
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C15 and C51 demonstrate systemic effects of MRP51 mis-regulation through polysome profiling showing reduced translation (24% decrease by amino acid incorporation, C51), and mass spectrometry showing enrichment of all quantified mt-LSU proteins (C14-C15), consistent with the expected consequences of reduced mt-SSU component Mrp51.

results.result: Cassette insertion at DBP1 causes respiratory growth defects that are general to multiple cassette types (kanMX6, natMX6, TRP1), demonstrating the phenomenon is not specific to a particular cassette sequence.
results.evaluation: Claims C16, C17, and C23 show that respiratory growth defects occur with multiple different cassettes (kanMX6, natMX6, TRP1) at the DBP1 locus, with growth curves demonstrating similar phenotypes across cassette types. This establishes that the off-target effect is a general property of cassette insertion rather than a cassette-specific artifact.

results.result: Bidirectional promoter activity from cassettes drives divergent transcripts that cause MRP51 repression, as demonstrated by orientation-dependent effects where reversed cassette orientation prevents the phenotype.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C27, and C30 establish the mechanism through orientation experiments. Reversed kanMX6 cassette insertion prevents respiratory growth defects (C27), and all observed divergent transcripts originate from the 5' end of cassettes (C30), supporting the model that bidirectional promoter activity drives the off-target effect (C3).

results.result: Insertion of transcription terminator sequences flanking the cassette promoter prevents off-target MRP51 mis-regulation and restores wild-type phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C24-C26, and C28 demonstrate that terminator-flanked cassettes (kanMX6-ins) prevent off-target effects. Growth rates are restored to wild-type (C24), Mrp51 protein levels are normal (C25), MRP51 transcript structure is wild-type by 5' RACE (C26), and the effect is orientation-independent (C28), providing strong evidence for the solution.

results.result: Divergent transcript production from cassette insertion is ubiquitous, occurring at 100% of loci in rrp6Δ backgrounds, but stable divergent transcripts are detected at only ~30% of loci in wild-type cells due to nuclear exosome-mediated degradation.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C29, C32, C58-C60 establish the ubiquity of divergent transcription. Analysis shows stable divergent transcripts at 6/20 (~30%) loci in wild-type (C29, C58) but 7/7 (100%) in rrp6Δ backgrounds (C32, C59), demonstrating that divergent transcription is universal (C60) but often masked by RNA decay.

results.result: Local sequence features, particularly NNS-mediated transcription termination and nuclear exosome degradation, naturally prevent off-target effects at many loci by limiting divergent transcript stability and reach.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C31, C61-C62 explain why only some loci show off-target effects. Divergent transcripts are absent or less abundant in RRP6 controls (C31), nuclear exosome is the major contributor to masking (C61), and the NNS pathway terminates and degrades most divergent transcripts (C62), establishing the protective mechanisms.

results.result: Use of minimal promoter regions in cassettes removes natural termination signals that normally limit divergent transcription, as demonstrated by experiments showing that longer promoter regions with endogenous termination sites or insertion of NNS termination sequences prevent off-target effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C36 and C63-C67 establish that minimal promoters lack protective features. S. cerevisiae pTEF1 naturally produces terminated divergent transcript CUT910 (C63-C64), but minimal short-pTEF1 causes stronger defects than long-pTEF1 with termination sites (C33-C34), and NNS termination sequences are sufficient to prevent effects (C35-C36), supporting the minimal promoter hypothesis (C65-C67).

results.result: The neighboring gene effect (NGE) identified in yeast deletion collection studies has been estimated to affect 10-20% of loci, but most cases remained mechanistically unexplained prior to this study.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C46 and C55-C57 establish the context of prior NGE observations. Previous studies identified the phenomenon (C44), explained some cases by regulatory overlap (C45), but left most unexplained (C46). Estimates suggest 10-20% of loci affected (C55), with genomic proximity being a significant factor (C56), but all prior examples focused only on kanMX (C57).

results.result: Natural LUTI-based regulation is a conserved eukaryotic mechanism involving bidirectional promoters, transcriptional interference, and uORF-mediated translational repression that temporally controls gene expression during meiosis and stress responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C43 establish the biological context for understanding the cassette-induced effects. Bidirectional promoters are universal (C37), transcription interference is widespread (C38), LUTI regulation involves both transcriptional and translational repression (C39-C41), occurs naturally in yeast (C42), and is conserved across eukaryotes (C43). These are well-established facts from cited literature.

results.result: Cassette-driven transcription interference is mechanistically distinct from natural LUTI-based regulation in that it does not require head-to-head orientation, continuous transcripts, or repressive uORFs, and can act over large distances.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C73 distinguish cassette-driven effects from natural LUTI regulation. Natural LUTI requires specific features (C70), while cassette-driven interference is less constrained (C71). Examples of natural transcription interference (C72) demonstrate it can act over large distances (C73), supporting the model that cassette effects can occur through transcription interference alone.

results.result: Cassette-induced off-target effects are difficult to predict from sequence alone due to multiple contributing factors including transcript stability, condition-specific expression, and local sequence context.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C78 establish the complexity of predicting off-target effects. Detection is difficult (C74), absence of stable transcripts is not diagnostic (C75), effects can be condition-specific (C76-C77), and prediction is currently not possible (C78). These conclusions are well-supported by the experimental observations showing variable effects across loci.

results.result: Even markerless genome editing approaches can cause off-target effects, as demonstrated by translation of novel ORFs in CRISPR/Cas9-based DBP1 deletion, emphasizing the need for complementation controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C83 extend the findings beyond cassette-mediated effects. Complementation experiments identified the unexpected regulation (C79), markerless deletions can also cause off-target effects (C80), as shown by novel ORF translation in dbp1Δ (C81-C82), demonstrating that even precise genome engineering requires careful validation (C83).

results.result: Selection-mediated genome editing using PCR-based cassette insertion has been widely used in yeast research since the 1990s and remains commonplace despite the development of CRISPR/Cas9 methods, though bidirectional promoter activity has long been known.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C49 and C54 establish the historical and practical context. PCR-based editing was pioneered in yeast (C47), used to create the deletion collection (C48), remains common (C49), and bidirectional promoter activity has been known (C54). These are factual statements about the field supported by citations.

results.result: Two-step strategies like Cre/loxP can prevent neighboring gene disruption but are labor-intensive and often not utilized, while single-step insulated cassettes maintain efficiency while preventing off-target effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C88 compare alternative approaches. Two-step strategies exist (C84-C85) but are labor-intensive (C86) and often not used even when loxP sites are present (C87), while insulated cassettes provide a practical solution (C88). The evidence for underutilization of Cre/loxP (C87) and effectiveness of insulated cassettes (demonstrated throughout) supports these conclusions.

results.result: The key features driving cassette-induced off-target effects (bidirectional promoters, transcription interference, termination mechanisms) are conserved across eukaryotes, suggesting similar effects may occur in other organisms including mammals.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C98 extend the implications beyond yeast. Key mechanisms are conserved (C89-C90), bidirectional promoters are universal (C91), termination mechanisms differ but serve similar functions (C92-C94), yet consequences for cassette design are not widely considered (C95-C96). The solution of adding terminators (C97-C98) should be applicable broadly. The inference to other organisms is reasonable but speculative.

results.result: MRP51 encodes a mitochondrial small subunit ribosome protein, and its loss leads to accumulation of free large subunits and affects global translation through the TOR pathway, consistent with known mitochondrial-translation crosstalk.
results.evaluation: Claims C50, C52-C53 provide biological context for understanding the phenotypes. MRP51 is a mt-SSU protein (C50), loss of SSU proteins causes LSU accumulation (C52), and mitochondrial dysfunction affects TOR and translation (C53). These are established facts from cited literature that explain the observed phenotypes.

results.result: Naturally occurring NNS termination sites may determine locus sensitivity to cassette-driven NGE, but prediction of these sites from sequence alone is difficult.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C69 identify NNS termination as an important factor (C68) but note the difficulty of sequence-based prediction (C69). This is supported by observations of short divergent transcripts at many loci and the effectiveness of NNS sequences in preventing effects, though the predictive limitation is acknowledged.

results.result: This study emphasizes the need for proper controls including complementation experiments to establish causality of observed phenotypes, even when using precision genome engineering approaches.
results.evaluation: Claim C99 is a methodological recommendation well-supported by the findings that cassette insertion caused phenotypes misattributed to the deleted gene. The rescue experiments in this study demonstrate the value of complementation controls for establishing causality.
